title: US tech giants' hidden AI debt swells 90% to $3.2T in 6 months
content: PALO ALTO, California -- U.S. tech giants' off-balance-sheet debt from artificial intelligence-related obligations continues to balloon, almost doubling in six months to about $3.2 trillion, with investors increasingly alarmed by seemingly unending spending.

report.summary: Off-balance-sheet AI obligations at U.S. tech giants surged roughly 90% in six months to about $3.2 trillion, alarming investors about runaway spending.
report.background: The AI boom has pushed hyperscalers — Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Oracle and others — into an infrastructure arms race: gigawatt-scale data centers, tens of thousands of GPUs, and long-term power deals. Much of that spending is structured so it never appears as conventional debt on the balance sheet. Committed but unfunded purchase obligations, take-or-pay power contracts, operating leases, and joint ventures or special-purpose vehicles with data-center developers and 'neocloud' partners sit in footnotes rather than headline leverage ratios. Add vendor financing and circular deals — chip suppliers investing in the customers who buy their chips — and the true scale of committed future spending becomes opaque. Nikkei's figure suggests these hidden obligations nearly doubled in just six months, a pace that outruns revenue growth and raises questions about accounting transparency as the market scrutinizes whether AI capital expenditure can ever earn an adequate return.
key_points: The number is enormous and fast-moving: about $3.2 trillion in AI-related obligations that sit off the balance sheet, up roughly 90% in only six months. That growth rate far exceeds the revenue AI products currently generate, which is why investors are starting to push back on 'spend at any cost' narratives.

Why it stays hidden: much of the money is committed rather than borrowed — multi-year GPU purchase agreements, data-center leases, power purchase contracts and joint ventures. Accounting rules let companies disclose these in footnotes as 'purchase commitments' rather than showing them as debt, so standard leverage metrics understate the real burden.

Circular financing amplifies risk: chip vendors investing in AI startups and cloud customers, who then commit to buying compute, creates revenue that depends on the same capital flowing round the loop. If one link slows, the whole chain can unwind quickly — a structure reminiscent of past telecom and vendor-financing bubbles.

Investor patience is thinning: the report frames growing alarm over 'seemingly unending spending.' Markets are shifting from rewarding AI capex announcements to demanding evidence of monetization, depreciation schedules that reflect real GPU useful life, and clearer disclosure of contractual commitments.

Depreciation and power are the next pressure points: GPUs age faster than buildings, and electricity contracts now run 15-20 years. Both convert today's headline capex into fixed costs that persist even if AI demand disappoints, squeezing margins for years.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes the boom as a leveraged bet: capability leadership now depends on balance-sheet engineering as much as research. Expect more scrutiny of footnotes, pressure for standardized disclosure of AI commitments, and consolidation as smaller players who signed take-or-pay deals struggle to fill capacity. Developers may benefit short-term from continued compute glut and price competition, but face risk of abrupt contract renegotiation, capacity clawbacks, or a funding winter if investors revolt. Regular users should expect AI subscription prices to rise as firms shift from growth-at-all-costs to margin defense, alongside slower model release cadence and heavier usage caps. The systemic worry is contagion: if a major AI infrastructure investor stumbles, the write-downs could ripple through chipmakers, utilities and credit markets.
report.tools: To track this yourself, use SEC EDGAR full-text search (efts.sec.gov) for terms like 'purchase obligations', 'take-or-pay' and 'unconditional commitments' in 10-Q and 10-K filings. OpenBB Terminal (open source) pulls filings, financials and estimates into one workflow; Alpha Vantage and Finnhub APIs offer free-tier fundamentals for building your own capex-versus-cash-flow screens. For power-side exposure, watch EIA electricity data and grid interconnection queues.
